items.title: Scientists propose ultrastable laser in moon crater for timing

featured_image.name: ESA - Telling time on the Moon

items.description:
A team of researchers from JILA, NASA, and Germany's national metrology institute has outlined a plan to deploy an ultrastable laser system within one of the Moon's perpetually dark craters, arguing the device could serve as a cornerstone for lunar timekeeping and help spacecraft land with greater precision.

The proposal, detailed in a paper posted to the arXiv preprint server this month, takes advantage of the extreme conditions found in the Moon's permanently shadowed regions, which are among the coldest environments in the solar system. Lead author Jun Ye of JILA in Boulder, Colorado, and his colleagues suggest that temperatures ranging from 20 to 50 kelvin, combined with the Moon's natural lack of vibrations and near-vacuum atmosphere, make these craters ideal hosts for a laser system that would outperform anything on Earth.[1][2][3][4]

"The whole environment is stable, that's the key," Ye told New Scientist. "Even when you go through summers and winters on the moon, the temperature is still between 20 and 50 kelvin. That's an incredibly stable environment."[1]

items.title: Microsoft warns US tech firms to 'worry' about Chinese AI subsidies

featured_image.name: Microsoft president raises concerns over Chinese AI subsidies

items.description:
Microsoft President Brad Smith is urging American technology companies to pay close attention to government subsidies fueling Chinese competitors in the global artificial intelligence race.

Speaking at the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi on Wednesday, Smith warned that US firms should "worry a little bit" about the financial backing Beijing is providing to its AI companies, according to CNBC. While acknowledging that the United States maintains "an advantage in terms of access to the most powerful chips in the world" and other technological innovations, Smith cautioned that Chinese government subsidies pose a mounting competitive challenge.[1][2][3]

items.title: Apple plans daily product announcements leading to March 4 event

featured_image.name: Rumor: Apple to Announce Multiple New Products in First Week of March

items.description:
Apple is planning to unveil a series of new devices through daily press releases during the first week of March, according to reports from Bloomberg and prominent Apple analyst John Gruber, culminating in a hands-on "special Apple Experience" event on Wednesday, March 4.

The tech giant is expected to announce the iPhone 17e on Monday, March 2, followed by updated iPads on Tuesday, March 3, and new MacBooks on Wednesday, March 4, according to Gruber of Daring Fireball. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman confirmed that this staggered rollout is "exactly" what he is expecting based on his sources.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Macron calls social media's free speech defense 'pure bullshit'

featured_image.name: The real questions raised by Macron on news media

items.description:
French President Emmanuel Macron sharply condemned social media platforms' free speech arguments during a visit to New Delhi on Wednesday, calling them "pure bullshit" in remarks that directly challenge a central foreign policy aim of President Donald Trump.

Speaking at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Macron argued that true free expression cannot exist when users are unaware of how opaque algorithms guide them toward content, including hate speech. "Some claim to be in favor of free speech — we are in favor of free algorithms — totally transparent," Macron said, according to Bloomberg. He added: "Free speech is pure bullshit if nobody knows how you are guided through this so-called free speech — especially when it is to be guided from one hate speech to another."[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Russian minister says foreign spies can read soldiers' Telegram

featured_image.name: Russia's occupiers had a 60-second Telegram kill chain ...

items.description:
Russia's digital development minister on Wednesday acknowledged that foreign intelligence services can monitor messages sent by Russian troops fighting in Ukraine through the Telegram messaging app, a striking admission that comes as Moscow intensifies its crackdown on the popular platform.

Maksud Shadayev said foreign intelligence agencies "are able to see messages" sent by Russian soldiers via Telegram, the Interfax news agency reported, according to Reuters. The statement provides an unusual official justification for Russia's escalating restrictions on the messaging service, which has become deeply embedded in the country's military operations.[1][2]

items.title: US sends 50 fighter jets to Middle East as Iran talks continue

featured_image.name: Middle East war fears ramp up as F-22 Raptors rush to keep the lid on Iran

items.description:
President Donald Trump has ordered a massive U.S. military buildup in the Middle East as nuclear negotiations with Iran inch forward, creating a dual-track strategy of diplomacy backed by unprecedented firepower in the region.

The USS Gerald R. Ford, the world's largest aircraft carrier, is now sailing through the Mediterranean after passing through the Strait of Gibraltar on Tuesday, according to U.S. Navy officials. The carrier is expected to reach strike range of Iran by February 20, where it will join the USS Abraham Lincoln strike group already operating in the Arabian Sea approximately 150 miles off the coast of Oman.[1][2][3]

items.title: Zelenskyy says US to monitor Ukraine ceasefire after Geneva talks

featured_image.name: US wants ceasefire only after framework deal, says Zelenskyy ...

items.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Wednesday that negotiators have agreed on American participation in monitoring a potential ceasefire, marking a breakthrough in military discussions even as two days of U.S.-brokered peace talks in Geneva ended with diminished hopes for a broader resolution to the nearly four-year war.

Speaking to journalists after being briefed by his delegation, Zelenskyy said all three parties—Ukraine, Russia, and the United States—were "constructive on the military component" of the negotiations. "They have, in principle, agreed on almost everything there. Monitoring will definitely involve the American side. I consider this a constructive signal," Zelenskyy said, according to Ukrainska Pravda.[1]

items.title: Microsoft unveils glass storage system lasting 10,000 years

featured_image.name: High-speed lasers write data — to last millennia — inside glass

items.description:
Microsoft researchers have published a study demonstrating a data storage system capable of preserving digital information for at least 10,000 years, potentially solving a looming crisis in long-term data archiving. The findings, published in the journal Nature on February 18, represent the first successful demonstration of reliable glass storage technology for writing, reading, and decoding information at scale.[1][2]

The research builds on years of work under Microsoft's Project Silica initiative, which uses powerful femtosecond lasers to encode three-dimensional pixels called voxels into glass plates roughly the size of a drink coaster. A single 12-centimeter-wide, 2-millimeter-thick square of glass can store 4.8 terabytes of data—the equivalent of around two million printed books or 5,000 films in 4K resolution.[3][2]

items.title: Iran builds 'concrete sarcophagus' over nuclear site amid US talks

featured_image.name: An Iranian nuclear facility is so deep underground that US ...

items.description:
Satellite imagery shows Iran is actively reinforcing its most sensitive nuclear and military installations, erecting what analysts describe as a "concrete sarcophagus" at one facility and burying tunnel entrances at another, as tensions with the United States escalate amid ongoing nuclear negotiations.

At the Parchin military complex southeast of Tehran, construction of a concrete shield over a new facility called Taleghan 2 has been completed and covered with soil, according to analysis by the Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) reviewed by Reuters. The site has historical ties to Iran's past nuclear weapons development program and may now house a high-explosives containment chamber essential for nuclear weapon testing, though Iranian officials maintain the country is not pursuing atomic weapons.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: US energy chief urges IEA to abandon climate work at Paris meeting

featured_image.name: Climate science-denying energy secretary nominee Wright ...

items.description:
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright urged the International Energy Agency to abandon its work on climate change at the organization's ministerial meeting in Paris on Wednesday, intensifying a standoff that could see America withdraw from the influential global energy body.

"I want to get the support of all the nations in this noble organisation to work with us, to push the IEA to drop the climate. That's political stuff," Wright said at the biennial gathering of energy ministers from more than 40 governments.[1]
